title: Python, Data Science & Machine Learning
description: A 14-week, hands-on path from Python fundamentals to an evaluated, shareable machine-learning capstone.

parts.title: Python Foundations
parts.chapter: Python Fundamentals: Syntax, Data Types & Control Flow
parts.summary: Write small Python programs with variables, collections, conditions, and loops.
parts.objective: Use core Python types and control flow to solve a simple data problem.

sections.title: Programs are instructions over data
paragraphs: Python values have types: numbers, text, booleans, and collections. Variables give those values names so a program can transform and inspect them.
A conditional selects a path; a loop repeats work. Together they make simple data-processing rules explicit and testable.
bullets: Use lists for ordered values and dictionaries for named fields.
Check edge cases such as empty input and boundary values.

sections.title: Turn a rule into code
paragraphs: A grade calculator is a small model of a policy: it accepts marks, computes a summary, and applies documented thresholds. Keep the calculation separate from the display.
bullets: State the rule before writing the condition.
Test values just below, at, and above each threshold.

visual.title: From values to a Python result
visual.caption: INPUT · TRANSFORM · APPLY A RULE · INSPECT THE OUTPUT

exercise.prompt: Compute the average of the marks and assign A (80+), B (70+), C (60+), or Needs review.
exercise.starter:
marks = [78, 91, 64]
average = sum(marks) / len(marks)
# Apply the documented grade thresholds
result = ""
exercise.hint: Use if / elif / else and compare average from the highest threshold downward.

quiz.prompt: Why should a grade rule check the highest threshold first?
choices: A mark meeting a higher threshold also meets lower thresholds.
Python only supports descending conditions.
It automatically sorts the marks.
quiz.explanation: The first matching branch wins, so checking the broad lower threshold first would mask higher grades.

parts.title: Functions & Files
parts.summary: Organize reusable code and read structured CSV data safely.
parts.objective: Write a function that parses records and computes a meaningful summary.

sections.title: Functions make work repeatable
paragraphs: A function names a transformation, accepts inputs, and returns a result. Small functions are easier to test than one long script.
CSV files store rows and columns as text. The csv module handles quoting and delimiters more safely than splitting each line by commas.
bullets: Use explicit parameters and return values.
Open real files with a context manager so they close reliably.

sections.title: Keep data and logic separate
paragraphs: A module is a Python file with reusable definitions. A program can import those definitions without copying code.
bullets: Validate missing or malformed fields before calculating.
Keep file paths configurable rather than hard-coded.

visual.title: A small data-processing function
visual.caption: CSV ROWS BECOME VALIDATED RECORDS AND THEN A SUMMARY

example.code:
import csv
from io import StringIO

text = "name,score\nAmina,84\nRafi,76\n"
rows = list(csv.DictReader(StringIO(text)))
scores = [int(row["score"]) for row in rows]
print(f"Students: {len(rows)}; mean: {sum(scores) / len(scores):.1f}")

exercise.prompt: Complete mean_score so it returns the mean of the numeric score values in the supplied CSV text.
exercise.starter:
import csv
from io import StringIO

def mean_score(csv_text):
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(StringIO(csv_text)))
    scores = [int(row["score"]) for row in rows]
    # Return the mean
    return 0

source = "name,score\\nAmina,84\\nRafi,76\\n"

quiz.prompt: What is the main benefit of using csv.DictReader?
choices: It maps each row's fields to their column names.
It trains a classifier automatically.
It encrypts the input file.
quiz.explanation: DictReader lets you address row values by column name and handles common CSV quoting rules.

parts.title: Objects & Environments
parts.summary: Model related data and behavior with classes, and learn why projects isolate dependencies.
parts.objective: Create a small class and describe how an isolated Python environment supports reproducibility.

sections.title: Represent a useful concept
paragraphs: A class defines the data and behavior of a kind of object. An instance stores values for one particular case.
Use a class when its methods make a coherent operation clearer; ordinary functions and dictionaries remain useful for simple tasks.
bullets: Initialize required fields in __init__.
Give methods one clear responsibility.

sections.title: Reproducible project setup
paragraphs: A virtual environment isolates a project's installed packages. A dependency file records what another learner needs to recreate it.
bullets: Use one environment per project.
Record Python and library versions for research code.

exercise.prompt: Implement Student.average so it returns the mean of the student's marks.

quiz.prompt: Why use a virtual environment for a research project?
choices: To isolate and record project dependencies.
To make every experiment statistically significant.
To replace source control.
quiz.explanation: Isolated environments reduce dependency conflicts and help others reproduce the setup.

parts.title: NumPy & Arrays
parts.summary: Think in terms of array shape, indexing, and operations over many values.
parts.objective: Compute row-wise and column-wise summaries while keeping array dimensions clear.

sections.title: Why arrays matter
paragraphs: NumPy arrays store same-typed values in compact, shaped blocks. Vectorized operations express one transformation over many observations without writing an explicit Python loop.
Shape is part of meaning: a matrix may represent rows as students and columns as assessment scores.
bullets: Inspect shape before applying an operation.
Distinguish element-wise operations from matrix multiplication.

sections.title: Practice the operation first
paragraphs: This browser exercise uses Python lists so it runs without installing packages. The same calculations map naturally to NumPy arrays and axis operations in a local notebook.
bullets: Use a tiny example to verify the intended axis.
Compare a loop result with a vectorized result when learning a library.

visual.title: Array shape explains the operation
visual.caption: ROWS ARE OBSERVATIONS · COLUMNS ARE FEATURES

example.code:
scores = [[80, 70, 90], [60, 85, 75], [100, 95, 90]]
column_means = [sum(column) / len(scores) for column in zip(*scores)]
print([round(value, 1) for value in column_means])

exercise.prompt: Compute the mean of each column in scores and store the three results in column_means.
exercise.starter:
scores = [[80, 70, 90], [60, 85, 75], [100, 95, 90]]
# Compute a mean for each column
column_means = []
exercise.hint: Use zip(*scores) to iterate over columns.
exercise.solution: column_means = [sum(column) / len(scores) for column in zip(*scores)]

quiz.prompt: In a matrix of rows=students and columns=subjects, what does a column-wise mean summarize?
choices: The average score for each subject.
The average score for each student.
The number of missing files.
quiz.explanation: A column corresponds to a subject, so reducing down each column yields one subject mean.

parts.title: Working with Data
parts.summary: Inspect, clean, filter, and group tabular data before modeling.
parts.objective: Apply explicit cleaning and grouping steps to a small table.

sections.title: A table is a data model
paragraphs: A pandas DataFrame labels rows and columns and provides operations for filtering, grouping, merging, and reshaping.
The browser lab uses dictionaries and lists to teach those operations without a package download. In a local project, the same workflow is commonly expressed with pandas.
bullets: Inspect data types, missingness, and duplicate rows.
Keep a record of each cleaning decision.

sections.title: Avoid silent data changes
paragraphs: A missing value is not always zero. Decide whether to remove, impute, or preserve it based on how the value arose and what the analysis needs.
bullets: Check the result after each transformation.
Do not leak information from held-out data into preprocessing.

visual.title: A traceable data-cleaning workflow
visual.caption: INSPECT BEFORE TRANSFORMING · CHECK EVERY OUTPUT

exercise.prompt: Group scores by team and calculate each team's mean in team_means.
exercise.hint: Collect each team's scores in a list, then average each list.

quiz.prompt: What is a sound first step when a new dataset is loaded?
choices: Inspect schema, types, missingness, and ranges.
Train the most complex model immediately.
Replace every missing value with zero.
quiz.explanation: Inspection reveals data quality and measurement issues before they contaminate analysis.

parts.title: Data Visualization
parts.summary: Use descriptive plots and summaries to understand a dataset before choosing a model.
parts.objective: Summarize distributions and identify patterns without overstating what a plot proves.

sections.title: Explore before modeling
paragraphs: Exploratory data analysis (EDA) checks distributions, relationships, outliers, and data quality. A histogram shows one variable's distribution; a scatter plot shows a relationship between two variables.
A chart is a question made visible. Choose axes and scales that make the comparison fair.
bullets: Label units and sample sizes.
Do not infer causality from a correlation plot.

sections.title: Make a useful figure
paragraphs: A useful visualization supports a specific claim and includes enough context to judge it. Compare the plot with numeric summaries and inspect unusual points.
bullets: Report missing values and exclusions.
Keep the plot tied to the population and data collection process.

example.code:
values = [12, 15, 19, 21, 24, 28, 31, 33, 37, 42]
bins = [0, 0, 0, 0]
for value in values:
    bins[min(value // 10, 3)] += 1
print("Counts for 0–9, 10–19, 20–29, 30+: ", bins)

exercise.prompt: Count the values in the ranges 0–9, 10–19, 20–29, and 30+.
exercise.starter:
values = [12, 15, 19, 21, 24, 28, 31, 33, 37, 42]
bins = [0, 0, 0, 0]
for value in values:
    # Select the correct bin and increment it
    pass
exercise.hint: Use min(value // 10, 3) as the bin index.

quiz.prompt: What can a scatter plot establish on its own?
choices: Whether two measured variables show an association in the plotted data.
That one variable caused the other.
That the sample represents every population.
quiz.explanation: A plot can reveal association, but causality and population generalization require additional design and evidence.

parts.title: Supervised Learning
parts.summary: Train a baseline model from labeled examples and evaluate predictions on held-out data.
parts.objective: Fit and inspect a simple regression model without using test labels for training.

sections.title: Learn from labeled examples
paragraphs: Supervised learning pairs input features with a target. Regression predicts a numeric value; classification predicts a category.
A training algorithm fits parameters using training data. The fitted model then predicts outcomes for examples it did not see.
bullets: Start with a baseline that is easy to explain.
Split data before fitting learned transformations.

sections.title: A line is a model
paragraphs: Simple linear regression predicts y as an intercept plus a slope times x. The slope summarizes the fitted relationship in this model; it does not prove that changing x causes y to change.
bullets: Plot residuals and check assumptions.
Keep test data separate until model choice is finished.

visual.title: The supervised learning loop
visual.caption: FIT ON TRAINING EXAMPLES · EVALUATE ON UNSEEN EXAMPLES

example.description: Fit a line with least squares
example.code:
def fit_line(xs, ys):
    x_mean = sum(xs) / len(xs)
    y_mean = sum(ys) / len(ys)
    slope = sum((x - x_mean) * (y - y_mean) for x, y in zip(xs, ys)) / sum((x - x_mean) ** 2 for x in xs)
    return slope, y_mean - slope * x_mean

slope, intercept = fit_line([1, 2, 3, 4], [3, 5, 7, 9])
print(f"y = {slope:.1f}x + {intercept:.1f}")

exercise.prompt: Complete fit_line to return the least-squares slope and intercept.
exercise.starter:
def fit_line(xs, ys):
    x_mean = sum(xs) / len(xs)
    y_mean = sum(ys) / len(ys)
    # Compute covariance divided by x variance
    slope = 0
    intercept = 0
    return slope, intercept

slope, intercept = fit_line([1, 2, 3, 4], [3, 5, 7, 9])
exercise.hint: Use the sum of centered x*y values divided by the sum of centered x squared values.
exercise.solution:
slope = sum((x - x_mean) * (y - y_mean) for x, y in zip(xs, ys)) / sum((x - x_mean) ** 2 for x in xs)
intercept = y_mean - slope * x_mean

quiz.prompt: Why hold out test examples until after model selection?
choices: To estimate performance on examples not used for fitting or tuning.
To guarantee a higher score.
To let preprocessing learn from all labels.
quiz.explanation: Repeatedly using test results to tune a model leaks information and makes the final estimate optimistic.

parts.title: Unsupervised Learning
parts.summary: Explore unlabeled data with clustering and understand what dimensionality reduction preserves.
parts.objective: Assign observations to nearest centroids and explain why clusters need interpretation.

sections.title: Find structure without labels
paragraphs: Clustering groups observations by a similarity rule. K-means alternates between assigning each point to a centroid and updating centroids to the mean of assigned points.
PCA rotates centered numeric features into directions that capture decreasing amounts of variance. It can aid visualization or compression but does not automatically make features meaningful.
bullets: Scale features when distance units differ.
Choose k and initialization carefully; inspect stability.

sections.title: Interpret with care
paragraphs: An algorithm always returns groups when asked, even if the data do not contain useful clusters. Validate the choice with domain context and sensitivity checks.
bullets: Describe the distance and preprocessing.
Do not treat a cluster label as a discovered natural kind.

visual.title: K-means updates groups and centroids
visual.caption: ASSIGN EACH POINT · UPDATE EACH CENTROID · REPEAT

example.code:
points = [1, 2, 8, 9]
centroids = [2, 8]
clusters = [[], []]
for point in points:
    index = min(range(len(centroids)), key=lambda i: abs(point - centroids[i]))
    clusters[index].append(point)
print(clusters)

exercise.prompt: Assign each point to the nearest centroid using absolute distance.
exercise.starter:
points = [1, 2, 8, 9]
centroids = [2, 8]
assignments = []
for point in points:
    # Append the index of the nearest centroid
    pass
exercise.hint: Use min(range(len(centroids)), key=...) to get the nearest index.
exercise.solution:
for point in points:
    assignments.append(min(range(len(centroids)), key=lambda i: abs(point - centroids[i])))

choices: Finds orthogonal directions that capture variance in centered numeric data.
Finds causal effects without assumptions.
Assigns class labels using a training target.
quiz.explanation: PCA is an unsupervised linear transformation based on variance, not a causal method or supervised classifier.

parts.title: Evaluation & Pipelines
parts.summary: Choose metrics that match the task and validate a complete modeling workflow.
parts.objective: Calculate classification metrics and explain how cross-validation reduces dependence on one split.

sections.title: Metrics answer different questions
paragraphs: Accuracy is the fraction of all predictions that are correct. Precision asks how often positive predictions are correct; recall asks how many actual positives are found.
A confusion matrix makes false positives and false negatives visible. In imbalanced settings, accuracy alone can conceal failures.
bullets: Choose metrics before inspecting final test results.
Report uncertainty and class prevalence when relevant.

sections.title: Pipelines protect evaluation
paragraphs: A pipeline binds preprocessing and prediction steps so each cross-validation fold fits transformations only on its training fold.
Cross-validation repeats evaluation over several train/validation splits. The folds are not independent studies, but they reveal sensitivity to one partition.
bullets: Keep one final test set for final evaluation.
Use grouped or temporal splits when observations are dependent.

visual.title: A leakage-safe evaluation
visual.caption: SPLIT FIRST · FIT INSIDE EACH TRAINING FOLD · TEST ONCE

example.code:
actual = [1, 1, 0, 0, 1]
predicted = [1, 0, 1, 0, 1]
tp = sum(a == 1 and p == 1 for a, p in zip(actual, predicted))
fp = sum(a == 0 and p == 1 for a, p in zip(actual, predicted))
fn = sum(a == 1 and p == 0 for a, p in zip(actual, predicted))
print(f"Precision: {tp / (tp + fp):.2f}; recall: {tp / (tp + fn):.2f}")

exercise.prompt: Compute precision and recall from the provided binary labels.
exercise.starter:
actual = [1, 1, 0, 0, 1]
predicted = [1, 0, 1, 0, 1]
tp = sum(a == 1 and p == 1 for a, p in zip(actual, predicted))
fp = sum(a == 0 and p == 1 for a, p in zip(actual, predicted))
fn = sum(a == 1 and p == 0 for a, p in zip(actual, predicted))
precision = 0
recall = 0
exercise.hint: Precision is TP/(TP+FP); recall is TP/(TP+FN).
exercise.solution:
precision = tp / (tp + fp)
recall = tp / (tp + fn)

quiz.prompt: Why put scaling inside a cross-validation pipeline?
choices: Each fold learns scaling values only from its own training data.
It guarantees the best possible model.
It prevents all class imbalance.
quiz.explanation: Fitting preprocessing before splitting leaks validation information into training.

parts.title: Neural Network Foundations
parts.summary: Follow the forward pass and a simple gradient update in a small neural network.
parts.objective: Compute a perceptron prediction and update a weight in the direction that reduces error.

sections.title: A neuron combines signals
paragraphs: A perceptron computes a weighted sum of inputs plus a bias, then applies an activation function. Neural networks compose these layers to learn nonlinear representations.
Training repeatedly predicts, measures loss, computes gradients, and updates parameters. Backpropagation applies the chain rule to efficiently calculate those gradients.
bullets: Weights represent learned parameters.
A lower training loss does not guarantee generalization.

sections.title: Watch the update
paragraphs: This tiny exercise uses one weight and squared error so you can inspect every quantity. Larger networks use vectorized calculations and optimizers such as stochastic gradient descent.
bullets: Track training and validation loss separately.
Use a learning rate small enough for stable updates.

visual.title: Forward pass and learning update
visual.caption: PREDICT · MEASURE ERROR · PROPAGATE GRADIENT · UPDATE WEIGHTS

example.code:
weight = 0.5
x = 2.0
target = 0.0
learning_rate = 0.1
prediction = weight * x
error = prediction - target
weight -= learning_rate * 2 * error * x
print(f"Updated weight: {weight:.2f}")

exercise.prompt: Compute the updated weight after one squared-error gradient step.
exercise.starter:
weight = 0.5
x = 2.0
target = 0.0
learning_rate = 0.1
prediction = weight * x
error = prediction - target
# Update weight using derivative 2 * error * x
exercise.hint: Subtract learning_rate times the gradient from the old weight.

choices: Gradients of the loss with respect to model parameters.
The number of classes in a dataset.
A guarantee that validation loss will decrease.
quiz.explanation: Backpropagation efficiently applies the chain rule to compute parameter gradients.

parts.title: Computer Vision & CNNs
parts.chapter: Convolutional Neural Networks for Image Tasks
parts.summary: See how local filters transform an image and how a CNN builds spatial features.
parts.objective: Apply a small convolution filter and describe the role of pooling and held-out image evaluation.

sections.title: Images are structured arrays
paragraphs: A grayscale image is a two-dimensional grid; a color image adds a channel dimension. Convolution applies a small learned filter across local neighborhoods.
Pooling reduces spatial size, and deeper layers combine simple patterns into richer features. A classifier maps the final representation to task labels.
bullets: Keep image dimensions and channel order explicit.
Split by source or subject when near-duplicate images could leak across sets.

sections.title: Evaluate the vision task
paragraphs: Classification accuracy is only one view of an image model. Inspect per-class errors, class balance, and whether train and test images reflect the intended deployment setting.
bullets: Use augmentation only on training data.
Check for background or watermark shortcuts.

visual.title: How a CNN processes an image
visual.caption: PIXELS → LOCAL FILTERS → FEATURE MAPS → TASK OUTPUT

example.code:
image = [[1, 2, 0], [0, 1, 3], [2, 1, 0]]
filter_2x2 = [[1, 0], [0, 1]]
response = sum(image[r][c] * filter_2x2[r][c] for r in range(2) for c in range(2))
print("Filter response:", response)

exercise.prompt: Compute the top-left response of the 2×2 filter over the image.
exercise.starter:
image = [[1, 2, 0], [0, 1, 3], [2, 1, 0]]
filter_2x2 = [[1, 0], [0, 1]]
response = 0
# Multiply corresponding values in the top-left 2x2 patch and sum
exercise.solution: response = sum(image[r][c] * filter_2x2[r][c] for r in range(2) for c in range(2))

quiz.prompt: What is a key property of a convolutional filter?
choices: It is reused across local image regions to detect patterns.
It assigns a unique independent weight to every image location.
It replaces the need for a test set.
quiz.explanation: Convolution shares filter weights spatially, which helps model local patterns efficiently.

parts.title: Sequences & Transformers
parts.summary: Compare recurrent state with attention and inspect how context weights combine information.
parts.objective: Calculate a simple attention-weighted context and identify what it does not prove.

sections.title: Sequence models preserve context
paragraphs: RNNs process tokens or time steps in order and pass a hidden state forward. LSTMs add gates that help retain or forget information over longer sequences.
Transformers use attention to calculate which input positions should contribute to a representation. Attention weights are model computations, not guaranteed human explanations.
bullets: Tokenization determines the units a language model sees.
Use time-aware splits for forecasting tasks.

sections.title: A tiny attention calculation
paragraphs: Attention scores are normalized into weights, often with softmax. The weights combine value vectors into a context representation used by later layers.
bullets: A weighted average is a teaching simplification.
Generated text still requires grounding and evaluation.

example.code:
weights = [0.1, 0.7, 0.2]
values = [10, 20, 40]
context = sum(weight * value for weight, value in zip(weights, values))
print(f"Context: {context:.1f}")

exercise.prompt: Calculate the attention-weighted context for the supplied values.
exercise.starter:
weights = [0.1, 0.7, 0.2]
values = [10, 20, 40]
# Compute the weighted sum
context = 0
exercise.hint: Multiply paired weights and values, then sum the products.
exercise.solution: context = sum(weight * value for weight, value in zip(weights, values))

quiz.prompt: Do attention weights automatically provide a faithful explanation of a model's reasoning?
choices: No; they describe a computation and need separate validation.
Yes; the highest weight always proves causality.
Yes; every model has identical attention.
quiz.explanation: Attention values can be useful diagnostics but are not automatically faithful explanations or causal evidence.

parts.title: End-to-End Project
parts.summary: Scope a capstone and connect data preparation, a baseline model, evaluation, and a usable demo.
parts.objective: Write a reproducible project plan that specifies the user, data, baseline, metric, and deployment boundary.

sections.title: Scope a useful project
paragraphs: A project starts with a user and a decision, not a model name. Specify the problem, data access, target, baseline, evaluation, and risk before building.
A complete workflow records data provenance, preprocessing, train/validation/test partitions, and the model artifact.
bullets: Prefer a small, measurable question.
Set a rule for what result would change your conclusion.

sections.title: Make a safe demo
paragraphs: An API wraps a prediction function with an input contract and an output format. Validate inputs and state what the model is not designed to do.
A local classroom demo is not a production service. Production requires access control, monitoring, logging, and a responsible fallback.
bullets: Keep secrets out of source code.
Document limitations beside the demo.

visual.title: A project from question to demo
visual.caption: PLAN THE EVIDENCE BEFORE BUILDING THE INTERFACE

exercise.starter:
def predict(features):
    # Reject inputs with the wrong length
    # Return the mean of the two features
    return None

result = predict([0.2, 0.8])
exercise.hint: Raise ValueError when len(features) is not 2.

quiz.prompt: What should a capstone proposal define before model training?
choices: The user problem, data, baseline, evaluation metric, and risks.
Only the neural-network architecture.
A target score chosen after test results.
quiz.explanation: A researchable project needs a clear question, data plan, baseline, evaluation, and risk boundaries.

parts.title: Capstone & Next Steps
parts.summary: Package a final result with evidence, limitations, reproducible artifacts, and a clear next step.
parts.objective: Save and reload a simple model artifact and communicate what the evaluation does and does not show.

sections.title: Present the evidence
paragraphs: A capstone report states the question, data, method, result, uncertainty, limitations, and intended use. A working demo is valuable only when its evaluation can be understood.
A saved model artifact should travel with its feature definitions, preprocessing, software versions, and provenance.
bullets: Include a simple baseline and honest comparisons.
Share code and data only when licensing and privacy permit.

sections.title: Choose a responsible next step
paragraphs: A Kaggle score or public demo is one feedback signal, not a substitute for appropriate validation. Career growth comes from a portfolio that shows reasoning, reproducibility, and communication.
bullets: Record what failed as well as what worked.
Check current venue, dataset, and deployment requirements before release.

visual.title: From capstone result to reproducible work
visual.caption: ARTIFACT · EVIDENCE · LIMITATIONS · NEXT QUESTION

example.code:
import json
from io import StringIO

artifact = {"slope": 2.0, "intercept": 1.0, "features": ["x"]}
buffer = StringIO()
json.dump(artifact, buffer)
buffer.seek(0)
loaded = json.load(buffer)
print(loaded)

exercise.prompt: Serialize the model dictionary to JSON text and load it back into restored.

quiz.prompt: What makes a model result reproducible?
choices: Code, data provenance, parameters, environment, and evaluation protocol are recorded.
Only the final accuracy is published.
The largest model is used.
quiz.explanation: Reproduction requires enough context to recover the data, procedure, parameters, and evaluation.
